p: Gladly. STOP has a report out on Fusion Centers, which I can link to in my written testimony, which I will be submitting later. It completely undermines it. It is a direct and opaque process by which essentially there is a deputization of anyone in that Fusion Center for ICE. Any information that is collected by any agency we have to assume is shared between every agency involved in these, you know, joint task forces, Fusion Centers, etc. These are the nexuses, if that's the proper plural, of the information sharing and the ways by which ICE gets a handle on our information. It makes legal defense or frankly even knowing what the case is and what's going to happen in the first place much harder.

Thank you, and thank you all for your testimony. The next panel we have is Michael Loeb, Christina [sp?] from– I can't read the last name fully, but from the Pro se Plus Project— oh, Krishna, sorry, from the Pro se Plus Project, and Lucky Ho from the Asian American Federation. You may begin.

My name is Michael Elan Loeb. I have a lot of friends who are immigrants. I come from a family of refugees and immigrants, and I'm at Federal Plaza at least once a week. Before I begin, I want to mention that in just one season, ICE agents have brought shame and negative attention to all law enforcement. So if I were a law enforcement professional of any type, I would not want to be in a position where my reputation or my safety had to rely on them at all. They're like an ethical negative Midas touch, and if a surge comes, we need to be ready to deal with that. Part two, when you get this wrong, the consequences can be extremely serious. So you cannot bring back meaningfully someone who has been deported and lost their job while they were detained or whose family is terrified. You cannot

repair those things. And part three, I'd say that DOC, NYPD, and ICE have three basic mandates: to enforce the law, to protect, and to serve. ICE's remit specifically to enforce immigration law. And I challenge any of you here to spend one full morning in an immigration court at Federal Plaza or a pro se asylum clinic and return convinced that U.S. immigration laws are just or transparent or being applied with anything less than caprice, selfishness, shortsightedness, and cruelty. So enforcing very bad law is very bad. And that is the case even before we talk about the tactics deployed by dangerous, hastily trained, and small ICE officers. They enforce bad laws badly. They should be abolished and all associated miscreants investigated. But that's not happening. So until that day, all safety personnel– safety personnel are rewarded handsomely to protect us and that sometimes happens, but many New Yorkers with justification don't trust the NYPD or DOC. We're rightfully cautious and can't leave anything to the decision-making of individual officers. And finally, to serve, the question is whose interests are being served? We saw disgraced former Mayor Adams take the

deal. We saw it. And he was willing to trade his own freedom and a handful of upgrades for our freedom. ICE, EOIR, and DHS officers serve the interests of elites who don't care about any of us at the pleasure of Secretary Noem and felonious Trump. So they're profiteering— profiting from concentration camps. We have sanctuary laws to keep the correct people, everyday New Yorkers, as the focus of service. Thank you.
Thank you.

Good morning. My name is Christina Garrity, and I'm the coordinator for the Pro Se Plus Project, a collaborative made up of four legal service providers and two community-based organizations. In the past three years, the Pro Se Plus Project, otherwise known as PSPP, has worked tirelessly to meet the needs of immigrant New Yorkers who are unable to retain high-quality legal counsel and must navigate our labyrinthine immigration system pro se. As I'm sure many council members are aware, people who are represented can appear in immigration court online, meaning that it's pro se respondents, the people our project is designed to serve, who have

been detained by ICE when appearing for routine appointments. Thanks to the flexibility of our project's model and the generosity of City Council, PSPP partners have been on the ground at 26 Federal Plaza and 290 Broadway since the courthouse arrests started happening. This has put us on the front lines of the Trump administration's assault on our collective right to due process and the integrity of our city's sanctuary laws. As my colleagues Tania and Benjamin have already discussed, we have seen firsthand the horrific consequences of the Department of Homeland Security's unprecedented expansion of unchecked power. This includes not only the violent unlawful detention of immigrant New Yorkers who are complying with reporting requirements, but a general undermining of our faith in public institutions. The fear created by the president's presence of federal immigration officers in courthouses drives community members who feel they have no other option to miss hearings and check-ins, precipitating orders of removal that will soon be impossible to appeal. If there is anything that our on-the-ground experience has taught us, it's that we can count on ICE to

willfully push the boundaries created by our local laws. When this happens, it is not only immigrants who lose, but all New Yorkers. To that end, I commend the committee's commitment to ensuring the NYPD and DOC's compliance with sanctuary laws. I close by insisting on the importance of funding services for communities most vulnerable to escalating detention and deportation. This includes not only PSPP, but pro se service providers in the asylum seeker legal assistance network and beyond. Thank you very much for this opportunity to testify.
Thank you.

All right. Good afternoon. Thank you, Chair Krishnan, and members of the Committee on Oversight and Investigations for holding this hearing and providing us with the opportunity to testify. My name is Lucky, and I am the Senior Civic Engagement Coordinator at the Asian American Federation where we proudly represent more than 70 member organizations and serve 1.5 million Asian New Yorkers. We also convene the Rapid Immigration Support and Empowerment Network, a network of nearly 20 Asian-led and Asian-serving organizations

providing immigration case management and legal service support to New Yorkers. As we've all talked about earlier, the current administration has brought drastic policy changes at the federal, state, and local levels. ICE's brute and indiscriminate tactics have shattered families, instilled fear, and prevented New Yorkers from accessing essential services such as law enforcement, public benefits, healthcare, and education. This is verified by our member agencies who have said that many of our community members have stopped accessing public benefits and even things like food pantries. They're just— yeah. And yeah, our New York City sanctuary laws are in place to protect immigrant New Yorkers, yet recent events indicate these protections were not upheld. In September 2025, a New York City corrections officer provided federal immigration officers with real-time information about the release of a man from Rikers. This led to his arrest by ICE. In late October 2025, ICE conducted a military raid on Canal Street in Chinatown, arresting nine immigrant vendors and five protesters. And then on November 29th, the NYPD helped ICE agents push

citizens out of the way while arresting more than a dozen protesters. Raids are only expected to escalate throughout the year, creating fear within our communities in the city. With a threat of militarized violence in our city and the lack of protection and training for NYPD officers, immigrant New Yorkers' rights continue to be violated and individuals with lawful immigration status continue to be detained without due process. As immigrant New Yorkers face heightened threats, we must prevent local and state law enforcement agencies from diverting resources to the federal deportation agenda and sharing sensitive information with federal immigration authorities. Here are our recommendations. We support the following recommendations to protect immigrant New Yorkers. Protect and expand funding for the following initiatives: legal services for AAPI communities, legal services for day laborers and domestic workers, and immigration legal services for survivors of violence and gender-based harm, expand investment in language-accessible legal services to include and prioritize case management as our CBOs act as a critical bridge, prioritize supporting small and

mid-sized CBOs serving emerging immigrant communities, and prioritizing addressing contracting issues that pose barriers for CBOs to promptly receive funding to deliver their crucial services. We must work together to make sure that immigrant New Yorkers are aware of sanctuary city laws and what that means for them. We also need to work to provide protections and options for immigrants to pursue when they are affected by unlawful cooperation between city and state agencies with federal immigration enforcement agencies. This is how we can assure that New Yorkers feel safe in their home. Thank you for allowing me to testify, and we look forward to working with you to make sure our immigrant communities get what they deserve.
Thank you all for your testimony. We'll now call up our next panel, Gabriel Rivera and Jennings Yusef [sp?]. Jennings, yeah. You may begin.

Again, at the wrong spot. I called your office, sir, this week, because I wanted to speak on a topic. It's a stalking issue, and I call the Deputy Speaker's Office because I

wanted to speak on a topic. One got back to me, the other one didn't. May 11, 2006, stalking issue started. I don't really understand, because 5,000 letters have gone to four presidents about all of this creeping around, and so I don't

And then last year–

Good afternoon and thank you, committee chairs and council members, for organizing this important hearing. My name is Nour Soubani and I'm testifying on behalf of the Surveillance Technology Oversight Project. I'd like to take this opportunity to highlight two initiatives that go hand-in-hand with strengthening the efficacy of the city's sanctuary laws by limiting the invasive monitoring of our communities by police, as well as information sharing with federal immigration enforcement. First, we must abolish the gang database and prevent data sharing with ICE. As was mentioned by my fellow panelists, the NYPD maintains a notoriously racist gang database that disproportionately profiles and criminalizes Black and Brown youth. One of the most serious concerns is information sharing with ICE. ICE often accesses municipalities' gang databases to conduct raids, then charge or deport the people they detain. A recent investigation uncovered that the New York State Police gang database has been merged into a federal gang database, which is then funneled directly to ICE and used to identify immigrants for deportation. We

urge the City Council to pass laws abolishing the gang database and preventing successor databases from taking its place. And at the very least, we must ensure that ICE is not given access to the surveillance profiles contained within this database. Second, we must dismantle the Domain Awareness System. The Domain Awareness System is a tool of pervasive and intrusive surveillance of New Yorkers. It links citywide camera networks, license plate readers, drone and helicopter feeds, ShotSpotter gunshot alerts, 911 and 311 call records, and other law enforcement databases into a single surveillance network. Every NYPD officer has easy access to the DAS on their smartphone and can share this information with federal immigration enforcement. In 2019, Documents revealed that ICE uses the DAS data to create watch lists tracking undocumented immigrants. The DOI's December 2025 report highlights just how dangerous the DAS can be in the case of Likhad Kurdia [sp?], where NYPD shared with ICE a DAS report—
Thank you for your testimony. Time has expired.
That included information on two—
[interposing] You can finish. If you can finish quickly, be good.

She's the reason that the sanctuary city situation is gonna keep on occurring for the next four years. We're gonna have more migrants in the city getting detained and deported, especially the low-hanging fruit are the deliveristas and the street vendors more because of this Police Commissioner. This Police Commissioner is a pro-cop and she loves Donald Trump. So the city council, like, going forward, I know next week we have the immigration hearing, and then we have the immigration for oversight, stuff like that. But starting you, Mr. Krishnan, you got to start calling for the mayor to fire Jessica Tisch, because once she gets fired, we will have a better— we'll have a better chance of

really making it– the city to the real sanctuary city that it should be. They're scared of her. I'm not scared of her. I mean, but these nonprofits like the WJP and Street Vendor Project and the NYIC, including city council, need to all come together and start saying the right thing is– fire Jessica Tisch, fire the
